items.title: What navigator.locks does and does not guarantee
items.body:
**Key: it serializes cooperating writers on one origin, so two tabs cannot both check the same old bytes.**

Without a lock, tab A and tab B could each read the same stored text, each pass the baseline check, and then each write, with the later write erasing the earlier one. The Web Lock makes the read-check-write sequence run one tab at a time, so the second tab sees the first tab's write.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Makes the write durable through a crash*: a lock controls ordering, not durability; nothing in `browserLock` deals with crashes.
- *Authenticates the tab or user*: the section title is literally "A lock is not authentication"; there are no users.
- *Stops other scripts or devtools*: the guide says a script ignoring the lock "can still modify localStorage" and a person with developer tools "can alter data". The lock only works for writers that cooperate by asking for it.

excerpts.quote: Web Locks serialize cooperating writers for this key on the same origin.
A script ignoring the lock can still modify localStorage. A person with developer tools can alter data.
return navigator.locks.request(STORAGE_KEY, work);

items.title: Why prices become integer cents once, at input
items.body:
**Key: math stays exact in integer cents, and formatting is an edge step that never changes the stored value.**

Decimal numbers like 39.95 are not stored exactly by computers, so adding and multiplying them can drift by tiny amounts. Whole cents (3995) add and multiply exactly. So `parsePrice` turns the typed text into cents once, at the boundary, and every calculation uses cents. `money(3995)` is called only to show `$39.95`; it returns a string and does not change what is stored.

Why the others are wrong:
- *JSON cannot store decimals*: JSON stores 39.95 fine; the reason is exact arithmetic, not storage format.
- *Lets parsePrice accept exponent notation*: the guide says `parsePrice` *rejects* exponent notation; its regex only allows digits and up to two decimals.
- *money() is slow, so results are cached*: nothing in the code caches formatted strings; formatting is simply kept at the edge.

excerpts.quote: `parsePrice` rejects exponent notation, negatives, extra decimal places, leading zero variants, and values above the permitted cap. Display formatting belongs at the edge: `money(3995)` produces `$39.95` without changing the stored value.

items.title: Why products are archived but discounts can be deleted
items.body:
**Key: receipts embed the discount's code and percent, so its history survives; products are archived instead.**

A receipt stores the facts accepted at checkout, including the discount details. So deleting a discount later loses nothing: the old receipt still shows its code and percent. Products are different. The reducer refuses to delete a product if any order line points at its id, and the error tells you to archive it instead. Archiving hides the product from new checkouts but keeps history intact.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Product deletion cascades into receipts*: it does not cascade; it is refused outright ("This product has receipt history").
- *Discounts are not shown on receipts*: the opposite; receipts embed them.
- *It is an oversight*: the guide calls these "distinct policies based on the chosen reference model" and says not to assume every delete should cascade.

excerpts.quote: Discount deletion is allowed because its historical code and percentage are embedded in the receipt.
"This product has receipt history. Archive it instead.",

items.title: Core idea: a requested change is not an accepted change
items.body:
Every edit in Buildgum travels the same road. The form keeps a **draft** (what you typed). Saving turns the draft into a **command**, a plain object that describes the change. The **repository** takes a lock, reads what is in storage right now, checks it, and asks the pure function `reduce` to build the next state. Only when the storage write succeeds does React show the new **accepted snapshot**.

Why care? Because the draft and the accepted state are two different things. If a save fails, the app must keep your draft so you do not lose work. And the code that decides what is valid (`model.ts`) never touches React or localStorage, so it can be tested without a browser.

A good exercise from the map guide: draw five boxes (form draft, command, repository, candidate state, accepted snapshot) and an arrow between each. Then mark where validation can fail (before the write) and where storage can fail (at the write).

excerpts.quote: The dependency direction is simple: the interface calls a repository, and the repository calls pure domain functions. Domain functions do not import React or localStorage.
The requested change and the accepted change are different objects.
Draw five boxes: form draft, command, repository, candidate state, accepted snapshot.

items.title: The safe order for search plus pagination
items.body:
**Key: filter and stably sort with an id tie-breaker, then clamp the page to the filtered count and slice.**

Two problems must be avoided. First, if you slice pages before filtering, a page can end up empty or half full while matches sit on other pages. Second, if two products share a title and the sort has no tie-breaker, the same item can jump between pages from one render to the next. So: filter, sort stably with a secondary key such as the id, clamp the current page so it is never past the last filtered page (an empty result counts as page one), then slice.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Sort by title only*: the guide asks "whether equal titles have a deterministic secondary order"; title alone does not give one.
- *Slice first, then filter each page*: the guide says to compute the filtered collection "before slicing a page".
- *Keep the page number fixed and show an empty state*: that strands the user on an empty page; the guide says to clamp.

excerpts.quote: Compute the filtered, stably sorted collection before slicing a page. Clamp the page against the filtered count, treating an empty result as page one.
Ask whether equal titles have a deterministic secondary order.

items.title: Why tab B is rejected even though its product did not change
items.body:
**Key: it is rejected: commit compares the complete stored bytes with B's now-stale baseline.**

Buildgum does not check one record at a time. When tab B loaded the workspace, it kept the raw stored text as its baseline. Tab A then saved a discount, so the stored text changed. When B commits, the repository compares the current text with B's saved text (`current.raw !== base.raw`); they differ, so the save throws "Workspace changed in another tab". The guide calls this deliberately conservative.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Succeeds because the product version matches*: the guide says B is rejected "even though that product's version is unchanged".
- *Succeeds and drops A's discount*: that "last write wins" bug is what the byte comparison prevents.
- *Merged automatically*: there is no merge in commit; it either matches the baseline or throws.

excerpts.quote: Even though that product's version is unchanged, B's save is rejected because its workspace baseline is stale. This is deliberately conservative.
if (current.raw !== base.raw) throw new Error( "Workspace changed in another tab. Export your draft, then reload.", );

items.title: Start here: how to read the Buildgum guides
items.body:
Buildgum is a small shop app that runs only in your browser. You manage products and discount codes, fill a cart, and record a *simulated* receipt. There is no server and no real payment. The point of the course is to follow one accepted change from a form, through checks, into browser storage, and back to the screen.

Read the guides in this order:

1. **README.md**: setup, and a table of the words the course uses (cents, record version, workspace revision, command, request key, receipt). Keep that table open.
2. **01-CODEBASE-MAP.md**: which file does what. Start with `src/model.ts`, not the big React file.
3. **02-CONCEPTS.md**: the five ideas the quizzes test.
4. **03-WORKED-CHANGE.md**: how fake checkout became a real local receipt, step by step.
5. **04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md**: what the tests prove and what they do not.
6. **05-PRACTICE.md**, then **06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md** only after you try the exercises.
7. **07-TRACE-LAB.md** last.

Tip: when a guide names a function, open it in `src/model.ts` or `src/repository.ts` and read the code beside the prose.

excerpts.quote: 1. Read [the codebase map](01-CODEBASE-MAP.md), then trace one create operation with the debugger. Locate where input text becomes integer cents.
Start with [the model](../src/model.ts), not the largest React component.

items.title: Why a finished merge still goes through the normal save checks
items.body:
**Key: another writer can act while the dialog is open, and the merge does not authorize persistence.**

A three-way merge dialog only helps the user decide field values. It takes time; while it sits open, another tab can save a change. So the merged product is just a new draft. It must be submitted against a fresh baseline, and commit must repeat the usual concurrency checks. The guide says it plainly: the merge analysis "does not authorize persistence".

Why the others are wrong:
- *Merge only covers titles*: the guide compares "each editable field", not just titles.
- *The dialog discards the original product*: nothing says that; the original is one of the three inputs to the comparison.
- *A completed merge proves no other writer changed anything*: this is the exact mistake the guide warns about: a helpful merge interface "does not guarantee that the world stopped changing".

excerpts.quote: Compare original-to-current and original-to-draft for each editable field.

This analysis does not authorize persistence. Submit the reviewed result against a fresh captured baseline and repeat concurrency checks at commit. Another writer can act while the merge dialog is open.

items.title: Why a matching retry after expiry returns the old receipt
items.body:
**Key: it returns the existing receipt: replay lookup runs before re-quoting against today's rules.**

Yesterday's checkout was accepted, so a receipt exists. Today's request carries the same key and the same details, which makes it a retry, not a new purchase. Because the repository looks for a matching receipt *before* it re-quotes, the retry finds yesterday's receipt and returns it. Expiry only matters for new attempts.

The guide lists the three cases that separate time rules from idempotency: a new attempt after expiry fails, a matching accepted retry succeeds, a changed payload under the old key fails.

Why the others are wrong:
- *It fails because the code expired*: that is the bug the ordering avoids ("could fail despite its existing receipt").
- *It is re-validated against today's discounts*: historical receipts are checked for internal consistency, "not whether the code is active today".
- *A new receipt at full price*: a matching retry creates nothing new.

excerpts.quote: Keep replay lookup before re-quoting a new request. Otherwise an accepted request retried after expiry could fail despite its existing receipt.
Historical validation checks internal consistency, not whether the code is active today.

items.title: Why commit checks for a replay before the baseline
items.body:
**Key: a retry whose acknowledgement was lost carries an old baseline, so it is rejected instead of replayed.**

When the first checkout was written, the stored text changed (it now holds the receipt). The tab that sent it still holds the text from *before* that write. If commit compared baselines first, the retry would fail with "Workspace changed in another tab", and the user could not get their receipt back. Running `replay` first finds the stored receipt for the same key and returns the current workspace, even though the caller's baseline is old.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Nothing changes*: the two checks reject different requests; a matching retry passes replay but fails the baseline check.
- *The lock is released early*: both checks run inside the same `lock(() => ...)` callback; their order does not change the lock.
- *Duplicate receipts*: with the swap, the retry is *rejected*, so no second receipt is written.

excerpts.quote: This can succeed even when the caller's baseline is old: the operation identifies an already accepted receipt rather than applying another change.
if (replay(current.state, command)) return current; if (current.raw !== base.raw)

items.title: Core idea: fast tests isolate the business rules
items.body:
Buildgum has two kinds of checks. The fast tests in `test/model.cjs` run the pure model and the repository with fake parts: an in-memory storage object and a promise queue that stands in for the browser lock. Because the fakes are under the test's control, rare situations become repeatable: storage running out of space, two saves racing, or a write that succeeds and then throws before the caller hears about it.

The browser checks cover what the fakes cannot: real React, real localStorage, real Web Locks, downloads and a second tab.

When you read a quiz scenario later (two tabs, a lost acknowledgement, a retry), ask yourself which test would reproduce it. That habit keeps you honest about what the code actually does versus what the screen seems to show.

excerpts.quote: Repository tests use an in-memory storage adapter and a serializing promise queue. A quota failure and two simultaneous stale-baseline saves become deterministic.
Browser checks cover React, actual localStorage, Web Locks, downloads, and a second tab on the same origin.

How to run the tests and the failure drills.

items.title: Why the request key is made when the attempt is frozen
items.body:
**Key: the client cannot tell a rejection from a lost acknowledgement, and a fresh key would create a second order.**

Picture this: the write to storage succeeded, but the tab never heard back (the "acknowledgement" was lost). From the user's side this looks exactly like a failure. If pressing Retry made a new key, the repository would treat it as a brand-new purchase and record a second order. Making the key once, when the attempt is frozen, means every retry carries the same key, and `replay` returns the receipt that already exists.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The key is a secret proving identity*: the concepts guide says the key "is an idempotency identifier, not a secret or proof of identity".
- *Avoids collisions on double-click*: the worked change gives the lost-acknowledgement reason, not collisions.
- *Key generation is expensive*: the key is made per attempt, not once per page load, and cost is never the reason given.

excerpts.quote: A retry with a *new* key after a lost acknowledgement creates a second order, which is why the key is generated when the attempt is frozen (Step 2), not when the button is pressed.
The key is an idempotency identifier, not a secret or proof of identity.

items.title: Why restore bumps the revision past both values
items.body:
**Key: restoring an old backup would rewind the revision, as if the workspace went back in time.**

The workspace revision is a counter that only moves forward. A backup file carries the revision it had when it was exported, which may be lower than today's. If `restore` simply kept the backup's number, the counter would go backwards. `restore` instead reads the current revision, takes the larger of the two, and adds one, so the result is always newer than anything seen before.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Revision equals the number of receipts*: the revision counts accepted changes to the whole workspace, not receipts; nothing in `restore` counts orders.
- *Makes restore idempotent*: the opposite; every successful restore advances the revision again.
- *Avoids decode rejecting seen revisions*: `decode` validates structure; the code shows no "seen revision" rule.

excerpts.quote: then advances the revision past whatever the import claims, so a reviewed backup can never silently rewind the workspace.
revision: Math.max(revision, imported.revision) + 1,

items.title: Working the 50% discount on 4,001 cents
items.body:
**Key: discount 2,001, total 2,000: one whole-percent discount over the subtotal, rounded half up to the cent.**

Do the math with the code. `quoteCart` computes the discount as `Math.floor((subtotal * percent + 50) / 100)`. Adding 50 before dividing by 100 is the classic "round half up" trick. Here: 4001 * 50 = 200050; plus 50 is 200100; divided by 100 is 2001. The total is 4001 - 2001 = 2000. The guide gives exactly this example and calls it a chosen business rule.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Discount 2,000 by truncation*: that would be plain `Math.floor(4001 * 50 / 100)`; the +50 makes it round half up instead.
- *Discount 2,001, total 2,001*: 4001 - 2001 is 2000; nothing adds a cent back.
- *2,000.5 stored as a float*: amounts stay whole cents; `Math.floor` returns an integer, and `money()` only formats.

excerpts.quote: For a subtotal of 4,001 cents with a 50% discount, the discount is 2,001 cents and the total is 2,000 cents.
const discountCents = Math.floor( (subtotalCents * (discount?.percent ?? 0) + 50) / 100, );

items.title: What reduce does when the price changed after quoting
items.body:
**Key: it re-quotes against the currently accepted catalog, sees the fingerprints differ, and refuses the checkout.**

The request key is new, so `replay` finds nothing and the normal path runs. In `reduce`, the checkout branch calls `quoteCart` again using today's catalog, then compares a fingerprint of that fresh quote with the fingerprint of the quote the client sent. The admin's price change makes them differ, so `requireThat` throws "Quote changed; review current prices before a new attempt." The user must look at current prices and start a new attempt on purpose.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Records a Cancelled order*: nothing is written; the throw happens before `next.orders.unshift`.
- *Accepts the old price*: that is exactly what the fingerprint check stops ("prevents acceptance under different terms").
- *Silently uses the new price*: the reducer never rewrites the client's quote; it refuses.

excerpts.quote: The reducer re-quotes against accepted products and discounts and compares fingerprints. A changed price, title version, or discount version prevents acceptance under different terms.
"Quote changed; review current prices before a new attempt.",
